analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurance to cover COVID-19 T-cell immune response tests at no cost to patients.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor vote; it sat in three House committees until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the existing free-COVID-testing requirement so that group health plans and insurers had to cover T cell immune response testing for COVID-19 with no copays, deductibles, or coinsurance. This type of test shows whether a person has had a recent or past COVID-19 infection. It was introduced in the House, sent to three committees, referred to a health subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Insured people would have gained free access to T-cell immune response testing for COVID-19 — useful for confirming a recent or past infection — instead of paying whatever copay or deductible their plan charges. Test developers and laboratories would have gained a guaranteed, paying customer base, since insurers would have had to cover the test.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured people seeking COVID-19 T-cell tests

how_it_helps.text: It requires group health plans and health insurance issuers to cover testing that assesses a person's T cell immune response to COVID-19.
That coverage must come with no cost sharing, so an insured person would pay nothing out of pocket for the test.
It amends the Families First Coronavirus Response Act, the law that already required free COVID-19 testing, to add this type of test to that free-coverage guarantee.

analysis.who_pays: Group health plans and health insurance issuers would have absorbed the cost of covering these tests without cost sharing, a cost that typically gets built into premiums paid by employers and enrollees. The mandate would have applied only to the privately insured, not to uninsured people.

drawbacks.text: The test at issue indicates a recent or prior COVID-19 infection, not active disease or immunity going forward, so its value to everyday medical decisions is limited compared with standard diagnostic tests.
Requiring plans to cover the test with no cost sharing shifts the cost onto group health plans and insurance issuers, which can flow back into premiums for all enrollees.
The bill reached only a subcommittee referral, so no committee ever weighed the clinical evidence, the cost to plans, or the design before the Congress ended.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — free T-cell COVID tests for insured people — would have been real but narrow: the test mainly shows whether someone had a past infection, not whether they currently need care, and it would not have helped the uninsured. The cost, a small increase in what plans and their members pay, was modest. On balance a reasonable consumer protection, but a small one, and it never advanced far enough to be weighed in committee or on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and then to a health subcommittee, and it never moved again before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Miller-Meeks introduced the bill on September 30, 2021, and the House referred it to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor committees.
On October 1, 2021, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, where most health bills wait for a hearing or markup.
No further action was ever recorded, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
It attracted only one cosponsor, a fellow House Republican, and never had a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer health plans came out ahead: they never had to cover T-cell COVID-19 tests without charging patients. Test developers lost a guaranteed insurance market, and insured people who wanted the test kept paying whatever their plan charged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

for.name: Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican with one Republican cosponsor [S4], and no member voted on it, so its partisan shape beyond that was never tested.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: They would have had to cover T-cell COVID-19 immune response tests with no copays, deductibles, or coinsurance, absorbing the cost or passing it into premiums. The mandate never took effect, so they avoided it.
A guaranteed no-cost-sharing insurance mandate creates paying customers for the test. The bill died, so no guaranteed market was created.
